paras: The lynching of Albert Williams took place near Columbus, Texas, in the last days of January or the first days of February 1881, when three masked men took Williams, a Black man arrested for horse stealing, from the man who had arrested him and killed him. His body was found with his hands tied and his skull broken, and a warrant was issued for suspected parties. Wire briefs carried the killing across the country as the lynching of a horse thief.

A man named James Walker arrested Williams, described as 'a negro', near Columbus and charged him with horse stealing. The Texas specials call Walker only the man who made the arrest, while the wire briefs call him 'the constable'.

On Monday, January 31, Walker reported that his prisoner had been taken from him. According to Walker, three masked men came out of the bushes, seized Williams and carried him off. The Galveston News correspondent wrote that 'little credence' was given to the story until the evening of February 2, when Williams's body was found near Columbus with his hands tied behind his back and his brains knocked out. A special to the Houston Chronicle placed the body about five miles from town and said his brains had been 'shot out'.

A warrant was issued for the arrest of the suspected parties, whom the Lancaster Intelligencer called 'the suspected murderers'. No arrest, inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage, and the suspects were not named.

The fullest account was a Galveston News special dated Columbus, February 3, which the Washington Evening Star printed on February 4 under the heading 'An Alleged Horse Thief Lynched'. The Savannah Morning News ran the same text the next day as 'The Fate of a Horse Thief' and repeated it on February 11, while the Dallas Daily Herald printed a separate Houston Chronicle special among its 'Houston Items'.

A shorter Galveston wire dated February 4 reached papers from Memphis to Yankton, Rock Island and Wheeling, under headings such as 'A Negro Lynched', 'Killed by a Mob' and 'A Horse Thief Lynched by a Mob'. It ran on February 5 in Sacramento, St. Paul, Cheyenne and Salt Lake City, and later in weekly roundups in the Fayette County Herald, the Perrysburg Journal and the Donaldsonville Chief, the last of which dropped Williams's name and said only that 'a Negro' was lynched for horse stealing. These briefs dropped Walker's doubted story and the warrant, and stated flatly that Williams was taken by masked men and 'shot dead'. As late as February 26, the People's Vindicator printed an unnamed version in which 'a negro horse thief' was taken from an officer by masked men and 'riddled with bullets'.
No Black newspaper coverage of the killing was found.

Accounts of how Williams died differ: the Galveston News special said his brains were 'knocked out', the Houston Chronicle special said 'shot out', most wire briefs said 'shot dead', and the Yankton Press and Dakotaian alone said he was 'hanged'. The Memphis Public Ledger's brief said he was taken 'from jail', against the Texas specials' account of a seizure from Walker on the road. Several briefs dated the killing to 'Thursday night', 'Friday' or 'the 4th', dates that follow the dispatch rather than the Columbus special.

reader.title: Lynching of Albert Williams
bases: A Black prisoner accused of horse stealing was taken from the man who had arrested him by three masked men and later found dead with his hands tied, and the papers headed it a lynching (A2, A6, A3, A13).

Albert Williams's body was found with his hands tied and his skull broken after three masked men took him from the man who had arrested him for horse stealing (A2, A1); the killing was outside the law, a warrant was issued for the suspected parties, and the wire called it a lynching of a 'horse thief' (A2, A13).

Two separate Texas specials, one to the Galveston News and one to the Houston Chronicle, agree on the arrest by Walker, the seizure by three masked men and the finding of the body near Columbus (A2, A1), and the Galveston wire repeats the core event (A3, A5).

framing.detail: Northern and western dailies ran the Galveston brief under headings such as 'Killed by a Mob' and 'A Horse Thief Lynched by a Mob', naming Williams as 'a negro' arrested for horse stealing.
The Galveston News special reported Walker's story with doubt, gave the condition of the body and noted the warrant; the Evening Star's headline called Williams an 'Alleged Horse Thief'.
The Savannah Morning News headed the same special 'The Fate of a Horse Thief', and the Lancaster Intelligencer called the killers 'the suspected murderers'.

conflicts.note: The two Texas specials describe the body as found; the shorter wire briefs condense. 'Hanged' appears in one brief only and is not supported by the Texas accounts.

record_check.dossier: Seizure reported Monday, January 31, 1881; body found February 2; February 4 is the wire dateline.
Seizure, binding and killing by blows or gunshot to the head; 'hanged' appears in one wire brief only and is not supported by the Texas specials.
Three masked men, unnamed; a warrant issued for suspected parties.
The county is not named in the coverage; Columbus, Texas is named.

info: Walker reported the seizure on 'Monday last' (by the calendar, January 31, 1881); the body was found 'last evening' before a special dated February 3 (February 2); short wire versions dated the killing to 'Thursday night', 'Friday' or 'the 4th', apparently from the dispatch date.
Near Columbus, Texas; the body was found about five miles from town.
Accused of horse stealing; arrested by James Walker, who 'charged him with horse stealing'.
Masked men, unnamed; a warrant was issued for 'suspected parties'.
